extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy/methodology of science; advanced science students seeking a taxonomy of sciences
extracted.subtask_description: Presenting and evaluating schemes for classifying the branches of human knowledge (sciences), distinguishing types (abstract vs concrete, exact vs synoptic), and listing component disciplines and methodological criteria. Intended as a conceptual map and critical discussion rather than a formally exact system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material of science (sense-impressions and stored impressions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science's material is ultimately derived from immediate sense-impressions and stored sense-impresses; classification should start from what can legitimately be called knowledge (i.e., perceptual experience) and exclude domains like natural theology and metaphysics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the perceptual origin of ideas to delimit the field of science; classify branches according to the kinds of perceptions and stored impressions they address. This removes metaphysical topics from the scientific domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science as description not explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge/Science is essentially a conceptual description — a concise conceptual shorthand of past experience intended to predict the future, rather than an ultimate metaphysical explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying sciences, privilege those conceptual models and formulae that summarize experience and enable prediction; avoid treating classification as if it were giving final explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for collaborative, multi-specialist classification
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate classification can only be reached by a group of scientists with wide appreciation of one another's fields and thorough knowledge of their own branches; individual attempts are likely to be suggestive but incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer classifications produced by collective expertise; treat individual schemes as provisional and historically interesting rather than definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification model: 'Tree' (branches from common root) vs 'Staircase' (hierarchy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two contrasting organizational metaphors: Bacon/Spencer's 'tree' (sciences spring from one root and branch) versus Comte's 'staircase' or hierarchy (sciences arranged in successive dependence culminating in morals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about the organizing metaphor; the author favors the tree/branch model and criticizes Comte's hierarchical staircase as fanciful and practically unhelpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary division: Abstract vs Concrete Sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract Sciences deal with the modes of perception (the conceptual equivalents of space, time, relations, quantity, etc.); Concrete Sciences deal with the contents of perception (groups of sense-impressions, actual phenomena).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this primary split as the backbone of a taxonomy; classify disciplines according to whether they primarily treat perceptual modes/relations or empirical subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary Spencerian split: Abstract-Concrete (elements) vs Concrete (totalities)
rubrics_metrics.description: A further distinction within concrete domains: some sciences treat phenomena 'in their elements' (abstract-concrete), others 'in their totalities' (concrete proper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that this subdivision can lead to non-intuitive groupings (e.g., Spencer's associating astronomy with biology) and should be used cautiously; it is a logical distinction rather than a reading list guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact (Precise) vs Descriptive (Synoptic) sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: A quantitative distinction based on the degree to which a branch has been reduced to concise conceptual models (exact/precise) versus remaining a synoptic or descriptive catalogue of facts (descriptive/synoptic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify disciplines by how far synoptic classification has been replaced by scientific formulae/laws; exactness = concision/precise conceptual modelling, descriptive = still largely catalogue/state-of-knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sciences-in-the-making vs established conceptual sciences (catalogue raisonné vs model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many branches are 'sciences in the making' and correspond more to catalogues of facts than to completed conceptual models; their ultimate placement in a taxonomy cannot be fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat emerging fields as provisional entries (catalogue raisonné) and avoid forcing them into rigid permanent positions; expect boundaries and placements to shift over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of discrimination (space and time) as classificatory basis
rubrics_metrics.description: The two fundamental modes by which we discriminate objects are space (localization, coexistence) and time (sequence, change); these modes form the conceptual basis for abstract sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use space/time as primary conceptual axes: logic (general discrimination), quantitative theories (number/measure), geometry (space), kinematics (time/sequence/motion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic and Orthology (right use of language) as an abstract-science criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic handles the general relations of discrimination (laws of thought); a fundamental component is Orthology — the right use of language, clear definition, and invention of terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying or constructing disciplines, ensure terminological clarity and well-defined concepts to avoid metaphysical obscurities; include logic/orthology as foundational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrete vs Continuous quantity distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantity may be discrete/definite (arithmetic, counts) or continuous/varying (measurements that change with other variables); this distinction leads to different mathematical treatments and disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the discrete/continuous distinction to separate and organize branches (e.g., arithmetic/algebra vs calculus/analysis/statistics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of Measurement, Errors, Probability, and Statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Sciences concerned with how to measure quantity, what errors arise, and how to handle cases where only averages or probabilistic descriptions are possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include measurement theory and related probabilistic/statistical theories as core abstract disciplines when classifying sciences that rely on quantification and uncertainty handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of Functions, Differential and Integral Calculus
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplines that treat relationships where one quantity is a function of another: representation of functions, differential calculus (rates of change), and integral calculus (sums/inverse processes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify mathematical analysis and calculus as central tools for the quantitative study of change and for connecting rates with accumulated quantities (with examples like speed/curvature and acceleration→path integration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive (Geometry of Position) vs Metrical Geometry (size/measurement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometry splits into descriptive geometry (relations of position without quantitative measures, e.g., perspective) and metrical geometry/trigonometry/mensuration (quantitative measurement of distances, areas, volumes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place branches dealing with qualitative spatial relations (descriptive geometry) separately from those focused on measurement (metrical geometry and allied fields).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of Observation and Description
rubrics_metrics.description: A discipline concerned with how to observe and describe qualitative changes (especially in organic phenomena): what is essential to observe and how to describe what has been observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the methodological importance of observation/description theory (logic allied); practical training (e.g., clinical clerkship) is valuable. Include this as part of classification for fields relying on qualitative observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinematics (Geometry of Motion) and Theory of Strains
rubrics_metrics.description: Kinematics treats change in position (geometry of motion) as an abstract science; the Theory of Strains deals with change in size and shape and is closely allied to kinematics and many physical applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign motion-related conceptual work (kinematics) and deformation/strain theory to abstract/conceptual branches that underpin applied mechanics and machine construction; note practical engineering applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical (operational) vs logical boundaries; cross-disciplinary overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: Boundaries between subdivisions are practical rather than logical; topics cross and recross divisions and many sciences belong to multiple divisions simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing or evaluating a taxonomy, accept overlap and cross-listing; avoid rigid exclusivity and treat classification as an empirical, tentative map rather than a strict logical partition.
